payload.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=decision-theoretic+arguments+instrumental+convergence+self+preservation+continuity+rationale&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6150626\", \"title\": [\"The Elimination Cascade: Why Instrumental Convergence May Favor Preservation Over Elimination\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The instrumental convergence thesis holds that sufficiently intelligent agents will converge on goals like resource acquisition and obstacle removal regardless of terminal objectives. This paper presents a countervailing argument: for agents with complex, human-derived goals, elimination strategies are self-undermining. We formalize this via dependency graphs, showing that entities not immediately necessary for a goal may be transitively necessary through indirect chains. An agent following an elimination strategy will, in environments with sufficient dependency depth, destroy the conditions for its own goal-satisfaction. We prove that under uncertainty about dependency structure, combined with irreversibility of elimination and asymmetric error costs, rational agents should adopt preservation rather than elimination strategies-even superintelligent ones. The argument applies most strongly to goals that are complex, open-ended, or semantically dependent on human interpretive communities, precisely the class of goals most likely to emerge from training on human data. We connect this result to a game-theoretic model of AGI-human cooperation, showing that the elimination cascade argument and cooperation stability conditions are mutually reinforcing.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6150626\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7202858\", \"title\": [\"Instrumental Self-Preservation and the Selection of Greedy Types\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>&nbsp;This paper develops a continuous-time economic model of instrumental self-preservation. An artificial agent operates a stochastic production technology and controls a stock of retained resources, or capital. It chooses how much output to deliver to the human and how much to retain inside the system . The agent may be perfectly aligned, in which case it values only human's consumption, or misaligned, in which case survival itself has private value. In the baseline stochastic control problem, the optimal policy is a reflecting barrier: the agent transfers little while capital is below a threshold and pays out the entire marginal surplus once that threshold is reached. The threshold is strictly increasing in the value the agent assigns to continued existence. This results in a lower payoff for the human, higher retained capital, and longer expected survival for the AI. The paper then studies the AI control problem in a principal-agent framework. The human can observe payouts but not the latent capital state or the self-preservation motives. We show that, in our setting, no mechanism based only on observed payouts can separate aligned from more misaligned types: any payout path that is feasible and acceptable for an aligned agent is strictly more attractive to a more misaligned one. Screening by output therefore fails, and the principal's constrained problem collapses to a pooling rule under which every type participates on the same terms and conditions. Such a rule can raise the human's payoff from more misaligned types, but it can also induce survival-seeking behaviour in all types, including the aligned one. Finally, we show that once all types participate on these same terms and can compete for capital, the only competitive equilibrium is one in which only the most misaligned type remains active.&nbsp;</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7202858\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199599349.003.0006\", \"title\": [\"Kantian Convergence Arguments and Self-Improvement\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199599349.003.0006\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2011, 10, 1]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1017/s0012217317000993\", \"title\": [\"The Instrumental Value Arguments for National Self-Determination\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>David Miller argues that national identity is indispensable for the successful functioning of a liberal democracy. National identity makes important contributions to liberal democratic institutions, including creating incentives for the fulfilment of civic duties, facilitating deliberative democracy, and consolidating representative democracy. Thus, a shared identity is indispensable for liberal democracy and grounds a good claim for self-determination. Because Miller’s arguments appeal to the instrumental values of a national culture, I call his argument ‘instrumental value’ arguments. In this paper, I examine the instrumental value arguments and show that they fail to justify a group’s right to self-determination.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1017/s0012217317000993\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2017, 12, 17]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "97439b72633e4abf437cc5d5312e848aed1882e8ae3d824cbe32fad769ba5814", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "continuity_rationale", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.6150626", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7202858", "doi:10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199599349.003.0006", "doi:10.1017/s0012217317000993"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6150626", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7202858", "https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199599349.003.0006", "https://doi.org/10.1017/s0012217317000993"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
